meta.title: A Data-Driven Framework For Space-Tailored State Of Health Battery Management System

abstract: The evolution of distributed space systems is increasingly mirroring the architectural transformation of modern automotive embedded systems, moving from rigid, hardware-centric designs to software-defined, intelligent platforms. In this shifting landscape, the development of autonomous satellite units requires onboard processing and decision-support capabilities to ensure service continuity while reducing the high costs associated with groundsegment operations. Central to these distributed architectures are energy storage subsystems; specifically, lithiumion batteries, which are subject to highly non-linear degradation and must be monitored with extreme precision under the harsh thermal and radiation environments of space. To address these challenges, this work introduces a State of Health (SOH) monitoring framework based on a supervised Machine Learning algorithm. The model is evaluated under different operating conditions to analyze its generalization ability. Recognizing the stringent computing power and storage constraints typical of space-grade hardware, the algorithm is optimized using pruning and quantization techniques, allowing sophisticated inference to run on resource-constrained microcontrollers. Finally, a specialized BMS architecture is proposed to host these compressed algorithms, providing a holistic solution that combines a predictive model with a real-world architectural blueprint. This study contributes to the realization of advanced, autonomous health monitoring for the next generation of distributed space missions.

blocks.html: The integration of satellite communications for Non- Terrestrial Networks (NTNs) has become a cornerstone of modern global connectivity, further accelerated by the rapid deployment of large satellite constellations and the decreasing cost of access to space. Concurrently, the push toward real-time Earth System Intelligence demands significant advancements in onboard Artificial Intelligence (AI) processing to handle complex data directly in orbit. In this scenario of increasingly autonomous and interconnected networks, it is essential to monitor the health of systems during their operational life, thus planning timely replacements [1, 2].

One of the most critical subsystems of a satellite is the Electrical Power Subsystem (EPS), which is responsible for generating, storing, and distributing the electrical power needed to operate all on-board units. Any degradation or failure within the EPS can directly compromise the mission’s operations [3].

At the heart of the EPS, lithium-ion batteries play a key role in storing energy and powering the satellite during eclipses. However, battery degradation is an inherently non-linear process that depends on operating conditions. For this reason, batteries must be carefully designed and monitored to ensure both mission success and long-term reliability [4]. In this context, a key parameter for assessing the state of degradation is the State of Health (SOH), defined as the ratio between the actual capacity and the nominal capacity of the battery [5].
In recent years, numerous methods for estimating SOH have been proposed. These approaches can generally be divided into experimental, model-based, data-driven.

Experimental techniques often require specific test conditions that are difficult to attain in real-world operating scenarios. Meanwhile, model-based approaches require precise parameter initialization, which is not always easily achievable in practice [6].

For these reasons, recent research has increasingly focused on data-driven methods that use historical aging data and Machine Learning (ML) algorithms to directly learn degradation patterns. Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) in particular have shown very promising performance thanks to their ability to model highly non-linear relationships, allowing for accurate estimations even in the presence of complex degradation phenomena [7].

However, there is still a significant gap between terrestrial and space applications. One of the most relevant aspects concerns the mission-specific requirements: satellites undergo repeated eclipse phases that subject their batteries to partial charge and discharge cycles. This scenario differs significantly from typical laboratory conditions, where batteries are generally tested with complete charge and discharge cycles [8].

Additionally, the battery consists of multiple cells connected in series and parallel, meaning that the degradation of a single cell can compromise the performance and safety of the entire pack. Without visibility at the cell level, early signs of degradation may go undetected. However, continuous monitoring of all cells generates large volumes of telemetry data, which cannot be fully transmitted to the ground due to bus and bandwidth constraints. As a result, it is necessary to process this data directly on board, transforming analog measurements into aggregate health indicators [9].
This challenge is compounded by a further constraint typical of space platforms: the limited hardware resources available in terms of computing power, memory, and storage capacity [10].

The contribution of this work is the development of a data-driven algorithm capable of operating on partial discharge curves, in order to reproduce realistic operating scenarios for space applications. Furthermore, to make the algorithm compatible with future on-board implementations, model compression techniques are applied, in particular pruning and quantization, to reduce its size and computational requirements. To assess the feasibility and reliability of the proposed approach, validation is performed using a lithium-ion battery dataset from Xi’an Jiaotong University (XJTU) [11]. Finally, a Battery Management System (BMS) architecture designed to host the developed algorithm is proposed.

The XJTU battery dataset includes experimental laboratory tests conducted on 18650 NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) lithium-ion cells. The experiments were carried out at room temperature and organized into six batches, each containing run-to-failure tests. The different batches are distinguished by the charging and discharging strategies adopted. For each batch, the main observables (current, voltage, temperature, time) and the SOH are reported for each test cycle [11]. Only two batches (each one composed by eight cells) were considered in this work. The test profiles are reported in Table 1.

blocks.html: In this study, the discharge curves are selected for the development of SOH estimation algorithms, as they are particularly informative with regard to degradation dynamics [12]. For each cycle the selected observables are voltage, time vector and current integral, which provide a smoother representation than the raw current signal.

Due to the impossibility of directly measuring the SOH in orbit and the consequent lack of labeled telemetry from space missions, laboratory datasets are currently the only available source for obtaining SOH values associated with each cycle. These datasets provide fully labeled data, making it possible to apply supervised ML techniques. However, the operating profiles used in the laboratory differ significantly from real ones in terms of the amount of data available per cycle.

To bridge this gap, this work proposes a partialization strategy aimed at emulating the State of Charge (SOC) intervals and limited data availability typical of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) applications from experimental laboratory datasets. To reproduce these operating conditions, for each discharge cycle, the initial SOC is set to 100%, a condition that frequently occurs at the end of an operating cycle to ensure that the battery is fully charged before the start of the next cycle. The final SOC is randomly selected at each cycle from a uniform distribution in the interval [10%, 30%]. For each observable, only the portion of the curve within the selected SOC window is considered. The SOH value associated with the complete discharge curve is then assigned to the corresponding partial segment.

The observable quantities are resampled to obtain sequences of fixed length and then normalized using Min- Max scaling. The pre-processed data is then fed into a Feed-Forward Neural Network (FFNN), chosen for its architectural simplicity and ability to approximate highly non-linear functions [13].

Considering the computational and memory constraints typical of space platforms, the trained model is then subjected to model compression techniques. In particular, a structural pruning process based on weight magnitude is applied in order to progressively remove the least relevant parameters from the network. Subsequently, the model is further compressed through quantization, exploring different numerical configurations to reduce computational cost and memory requirements while maintaining adequate predictive performance.

The analyses were carried out using an FFNN, composed of three hidden layers with 64 neurons each and ReLU activation functions. The model is trained by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) using the Adam optimizer, with a learning rate of 10−3 and weight decay of 10−4. Training is performed with a batch size of 16 for 500 epochs, applying a 5% dropout to mitigate overfitting phenomena.

The performance of the developed model is evaluated in terms of its generalization ability. Specifically, one set of data is used for training, while a different set is used for testing. This scenario reflects realistic conditions in which the telemetry acquired during the mission may differ from the controlled profiles used in the laboratory for training. The SOH estimation accuracy is evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and the coefficient of determination
Computational costs are also evaluated for potential on-board use, considering model complexity (number of parameters), inference cost (FLOPs), and non-volatile memory requirements (model file size).
All experiments were performed on a CPU-based platform equipped with an Intel Xeon processor (2.0–2.3 GHz) and approximately 12 GB of available RAM.

To fit the hardware constraints of space platforms, the model was compressed using pruning and quantization. Specifically, we used the Torch-Pruning library [15] to apply global magnitude pruning, which progressively removes the smallest absolute weights across the entire network. The process is divided into five iterative steps, distributed during the initial training phase, in order to gradually achieve the desired level of sparsity while maintaining training stability. The output layer was excluded from the pruning process to preserve the model’s regressive capacity. Three levels of parameter reduction were considered: 20%, 50%, and 77%. Subsequently, the pruned models were evaluated using different numerical precisions: FP32, FP16, and INT8, performed using Quantization Aware Training (QAT), in order to preserve the model’s performance as much as possible [16].

blocks.html: Table 2 compares, in terms of estimation performance and computational cost, the baseline model with different compressed versions obtained through structural pruning and quantization. The nomenclature of the compressed models follows the structure: ParametersReduction_QuantizationType where ParametersReduction indicates the percentage of parameters removed through pruning, while QuantizationType represents the numerical precision used. As can be seen, reducing the parameters by 20% causes a slight reduction in accuracy, but there is a significant improvement in memory use compared to the baseline. It is interesting to note that FP16 quantization does not introduce significant degradation in performance, suggesting that 16-bit numerical precision is sufficient to effectively represent the model weights. In contrast, INT8 quantization leads to a slight additional loss, but allows for a much more pronounced reduction in memory. With a 50% reduction in parameters, the performance degradation remains relatively small. This behavior suggests that the baseline model has some parametric redundancy. In other words, a significant portion of the weights contribute marginally to the regressive capacity and can be removed without drastically compromising the quality of the estimates. In the case of a 77% reduction, the impact on accuracy becomes more evident. This deterioration is consistent with the progressive loss of the network’s representative capacity. However, from a compression point of view, this configuration represents the upper threshold at which the network maintains reasonable performance while minimizing computational and memory requirements. It can also be observed that, with the same pruning, the variation in numerical precision produces relatively limited variations in model performance. This behavior indicates that even an INT8 representation is generally sufficient to capture the battery degradation process, provided that the pruning level is not excessively high. This behavior is best illustrated by examining Figure 1. In particular, one can see that pruning dominates the trend of R2, while quantization introduces more limited variations. All curves show a progressive decrease in R2 as network sparsity increases, with a particularly noticeable drop in the transition from 50% to 77% pruning. The FP16 configuration consistently outperforms the FP32 version for all pruning levels, which is an interesting finding. This behavior suggests that the reduction in numerical precision may implicitly act as a form of regularization, limiting overfitting and slightly improving the model’s generalization capacity. In contrast, INT8 quantization shows a more noticeable degradation, although it remains limited for moderate pruning levels. The relationship between compression ratio (estimated considering pruning and quantization) [17] and accuracy is also shown. This representation shows how configurations with high compression levels can still maintain relatively high accuracy, demonstrating that a significant reduction in resource requirements can be achieved without drastically compromising performance.

In the proposed system architecture, battery health monitoring and prognostics are structured as a functional stack that separates low-level sensing, health estimation, forecasting, and mission-level decision-making. This approach addresses a critical gap in current spacecraft designs, where direct information on SOH and SOC is notoriously limited, and the interfacing between power subsystems and the On-Board Computer (OBC) is often cumbersome, relying on fragmented telemetry that lacks real-time diagnostic depth.

At the lowest layer, the smart BMS performs raw telemetry acquisition through dedicated analog front-ends and ADCs interfaced to current, voltage, and temperature sensors embedded within the power subsystem. Unlike traditional architectures that burden the primary bus with raw data, these measurements remain resident only in volatile memory inside the BMS. Here, they are processed by an embedded microcontroller implementing the neuralnetwork-based SOH estimator described earlier. Nominally, the BMS exposes only the resulting SOH values and associated diagnostic flags to the OBC, significantly streamlining the interfacing process and reducing bus and storage requirements.

The communication between the BMS and OBC follows modern, high-speed spaceborne interfaces such as SpaceWire, CAN, or Ethernet, ensuring compatibility with contemporary spacecraft avionics while moving away from the restrictive, legacy serial links of the past. Above this diagnostic layer, the OBC hosts a persistent SOH history manager responsible for maintaining a long-term, nonvolatile record of health trends over the mission lifetime.

This historical database serves as input to the next functional layer: the Remaining Useful Life (RUL) estimation module. Depending on the processing capabilities of the platform, this module can either be executed on-board, leveraging hardware accelerators, or delegated to ground processing. The RUL predictor uses the streamed SOH estimates and their temporal evolution to run forecasting algorithms. Finally, at the top of the functional stack, SOH and RUL information are utilized as critical inputs for autonomous mission planning and scheduling, ensuring the spacecraft can proactively manage its energy budget based on actual battery degradation.

The results presented highlight how the proposed model manages to maintain good SOH estimation accuracy even when there is a significant reduction in network complexity. The combined application of pruning and quantization techniques demonstrates that it is possible to obtain extremely compact models, with memory requirements and computational costs compatible with the typical limitations of the hardware used in space platforms. This suggests that relatively small neural networks can be effectively integrated into the proposed Battery Management System architecture, allowing advanced diagnostic algorithms to be executed directly on board the satellite. Furthermore, experiments conducted on set different from those used for training indicate a good generalization capacity of the model.
Despite these promising results, deploying these data-driven models in operational spaceflight requires addressing several critical system-level issues:

• Architectural Fragmentation: In current spacecraft designs, direct information on SOH and SOC is notoriously limited, and the interfacing between power subsystems and the OBC is often cumbersome. These legacy architectures frequently rely on fragmented telemetry that lacks real-time diagnostic depth.

• Uncertainty in Autonomous Decisions: The accuracy of the SOH estimate alone may not be sufficient. For applications related to RUL prediction, it becomes crucial to also consider the robustness of the estimates and the quantification of the uncertainty associated with the predictions in order to reliably support decision-making processes.

• Explainable AI (XAI) Integration: As these systems transition toward autonomous decision-making, the inherent opacity of complex neural networks must be addressed to ensure operator trust and system reliability.
